claims.text: At Furuviksparken, five captive-born adult white-faced sakis (three females and two males) were individually offered all 105 pairwise combinations of 15 familiar foods from their human-care diet, with each pair presented ten times. Their group preference ranking correlated positively with the foods' total energy content; among carbohydrates, protein, and lipids, lipid content showed the strongest positive correlation. The 5,250 choices were repeated presentations to the same five animals. The authors state that this small zoo sample cannot support species-level generalization and does not represent feeding by wild individuals.

claims.lifeStatus: All five participants were captive-born and housed under human care; no wild animals were included.

gaps: Evidence is from one zoo group of five animals and repeated choice trials using provisioned foods; no wild diet, natural resource use, habitat interaction, or species-wide feeding pattern is established.
No species-specific phylogenetic or comparative evolutionary analysis was assessed.
The zoo study site is not a native-range record; no distribution source was reviewed.
No fossil evidence or bounded fossil-record search was assessed.
No current assessment, population trend, or threat analysis was reviewed.

reasons: One small captive food-choice experiment supports only a tightly bounded ecology claim.
Six facets remain not assessed; the source explicitly cautions against species-level generalization.
No multi-source species review or independent external expert review has been completed.
